---
title: "Does metacommunity assembly leave a trace in branch rates?"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4)
library(ggplot2)
res <- readRDS("rates-assembly.rds")
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
# "k of n" from a rejection rate and the number of replicates
kn <- function(rate, n) paste(round(rate * n), "of", n)
es <- res$essim
es_d <- function(b, col = "es_tau") es[es$link == "dispersal" & es$b == b, col]
n_d <- es$n[es$link == "dispersal"][1]
jd <- res$januario[res$januario$link == "dispersal" & res$januario$window == 30, ]
tb <- res$turnover
```

Metacommunity ecology and macroevolution have mostly been studied apart, although local
adaptation and community assembly can change speciation and extinction and, through them,
the shape of phylogenies (Leibold et al. 2022). Models of speciation in metacommunities link
spatial structure and dispersal to diversification (Hubert et al. 2015), and the evolution of
traits within communities feeds back on their assembly (McPeek 2017). Januario et al. (2025)
tested one link of this kind, between the metapopulation persistence of species and their tip
speciation rates, and found none. Two mechanisms could produce such a decoupling. Evolution
mediated by priority effects can make species equivalent at the regional scale, so that
properties of local dynamics do not translate into differences among species (Leibold et al.
2019), and local evolution often dampens spatial patterns (Urban et al. 2020). From these two
mechanisms we derive a working hypothesis of our own: adaptive divergence driven by local
dynamics stays among populations, so its trace should be weak in rates estimated among
species and strong in trait variation among populations. However, these studies deal with
ecological patterns or with rates of diversification, and none uses rates of trait evolution
per branch, so the link to branch rates is our interpretation. Moreover, a negative result
from a test with low power cannot distinguish a decoupling from a failure to detect.

This article asks, with simulations in which the truth is known, what can be recovered at
each scale. We ask (i) how well branch rates of trait evolution are identified at all, (ii)
whether an assembly signal planted in branch rates is recovered, (iii) whether local
adaptation and character displacement are recovered from trait variation among individuals
and populations, and (iv) whether a regression of tip speciation rates on persistence, as in
Januario et al. (2025), has power to detect a causal link. It is a study of recovery, not of
causation. In the simulations, local adaptation and character displacement act when
individuals are sampled and do not evolve during the dynamics, branch rates are set by
`turnover_rates()` from the history of each lineage, and the two layers do not share the
trait. Whether assembly *causes* the rates of trait evolution needs traits that evolve within
the metacommunity, which comdynamite does not yet simulate (see Limitations). The tutorial on
the generators used here is in `vignette("branch-rates")`.

## Branch rates are weakly identified

With one realisation of the process per branch, the rate of a branch and the change along it
are different quantities, and an estimator that reads one change per branch can at best
follow the change. We simulated traits on trees of 60 tips with `trait_rates()` under three
models of rate variation and estimated rates per branch with RRphylo (Castiglione et al.
2018). The correlation between true change and true rate, which bounds what such an estimator
can recover, had medians below 0.4 in all three models (Table 1). RRphylo followed the
realised change (median Spearman correlation
`r f2(min(res$rrphylo$with_change))`–`r f2(max(res$rrphylo$with_change))`) but hardly followed
the true rate (`r f2(min(res$rrphylo$with_rate))`–`r f2(max(res$rrphylo$with_rate))`). Methods
that pool branches within rate regimes are not bound in this way. BAMM (Rabosky 2014), fitted
to `r res$bamm$replicates` trees of 100 tips simulated with rate shifts drawn as in its own
prior (shifts by a Poisson process, each multiplying or dividing the rate by 6), reached a
median Spearman correlation of `r f2(res$bamm$spearman)` between posterior mean and true rate
per branch, and gave a marginal probability of a shift of `r f2(res$bamm$prob_shift)` on
branches with a true shift against `r f2(res$bamm$prob_none)` on the others. The two
experiments differ in tree size and generating model, so they are not a contest between the
methods. As a result, even a perfect link between assembly and rates would be seen through a
noisy estimate, which is less noisy when rates change in discrete regimes.

```{r}
rr <- res$rrphylo
rr$model <- c(gbm = "Brownian log rate", iid = "lognormal per branch",
              shift = "inherited shifts")[rr$model]
knitr::kable(setNames(rr, c("model", "with change", "with rate", "ceiling")),
             digits = 2,
             caption = paste("Table 1. Median Spearman correlation of the RRphylo rate per",
                             "branch with the true change and the true rate, and the",
                             "correlation between true change and true rate (ceiling),",
                             "for three models of rate variation in trait_rates()."))
```

## A planted trace is weakly recovered among species

We then planted the trace. We simulated `r res$n_metacommunities` metacommunities, each with
30 species on a 10 × 10 grid for 600 steps. They crossed dispersal (0.001, 0.01, 0.1), patch
extirpation (0, 0.01, 0.05) and two levels of spatial autocorrelation of the environment, with
20 replicates per cell. In each, `turnover_rates()` set the rate of each tip branch to
increase linearly with the turnover of its interaction partners over the last 0.1 time units
of the branch (k = 100), with internal branches at the base rate, and the trait evolved with
these rates. The rate of a tip therefore also depends on the length of its branch. The
Spearman correlation between the RRphylo rate of the tips and partner turnover averaged
`r f2(min(tb$rho_turnover[tb$n >= 10]))`–`r f2(max(tb$rho_turnover[tb$n >= 10]))` across cells
(Fig. 1). Only the cell with the lowest dispersal and no extirpation stood out, with a lower
value, since cell means have a standard error of about 0.03. With the lowest dispersal and the
highest extirpation, populations hardly co-occurred: displacement could not be fitted in any
of the `r tb$n_sims[1]` metacommunities of that cell, and only
`r tb$n[tb$dispersal == 0.001 & tb$extirpation == 0.05]` gave a correlation for branch rates.
These values hold for this map from turnover to rate, trees of 30 tips and RRphylo; a stronger
map or larger trees would give higher correlations, so the experiment shows a favourable but
not a limiting case.

```{r, fig.cap = "Fig. 1. Mean Spearman correlation between the RRphylo rate of the tips and the turnover of interaction partners that set their true rates, across dispersal and patch extirpation (40 metacommunities per cell). Note that no cell exceeds 0.2; the grey cell had only 8 metacommunities with populations left to analyse."}
tb$label <- ifelse(tb$n >= 10, f2(tb$rho_turnover), paste0("n = ", tb$n))
tb$fill <- ifelse(tb$n >= 10, tb$rho_turnover, NA)
ggplot(tb, aes(factor(dispersal), factor(extirpation), fill = fill)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#2171b5", limits = c(0, 0.3),
                      na.value = "grey85", name = "Spearman") +
  labs(x = "Dispersal", y = "Patch extirpation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## The signal is recovered among populations

From the same metacommunities, we sampled individuals with `sample_individuals()`, giving
populations a response to the environment of their site (local adaptation, $h$ = 0 or 0.5)
and a push away from co-occurring species (character displacement, $c$ = 0, 1 or 3), with
20 or 100 sites and 5 or 20 individuals per population. Two tools were compared: the
T-statistics of Violle et al. (2012), with `tstats()`, and the joint fit of $h$ and $c$ to
population means by `population_shifts()`, which follows Goldberg & Lande (2006) and Adams &
Collyer (2007) in assessing divergence among sympatric species after removing the
environmental gradient.

The T-statistics alone do not separate the two processes, because they act in opposite
directions on the variance within communities. Local adaptation makes co-occurring
populations converge on the environment of their site and raises $T_{IP/IC}$, whereas
displacement makes them diverge and lowers it. With the null model that exchanges population
means among populations of the same species (`null_ip = "species"`), which keeps composition,
abundances and variances within populations, the standardised effect size of $T_{IP/IC}$ was
near zero without either process and strongly positive with local adaptation alone. Adding
displacement reduced it, and with $c$ = 3 it was close to zero (Table 2). Interestingly, the
combination of local adaptation and strong displacement looks like no process at all. By
construction, the null that permutes individuals within sites (Taudière & Violle 2016) asks
only whether populations differ, so it would return a negative effect whenever co-occurring
species have different means. We did not find this species-restricted null in the literature
on T-statistics, although our search was not exhaustive.

```{r}
ts <- res$tstats
ts <- ts[order(ts$h, ts$c), ]
knitr::kable(setNames(ts, c("h", "c", "SES T_IP/IC", "SES T_PC/PR")), digits = 2,
             row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("Table 2. Mean standardised effect size of two T-statistics",
                             "against the species-restricted null (100 sites, 20 individuals",
                             "per population)."))
```

`population_shifts()` recovered $h$ in every design (root mean square error
`r f2(min(res$h_rmse$rmse_h))`–`r f2(max(res$h_rmse$rmse_h))`). Power for $c$ = 1, against
the 95% quantile of $\hat c$ under $c$ = 0 in the same cell (20 values per cell, so the
thresholds are approximate), averaged
`r f2(res$power_c_design$power.mean[res$power_c_design$design == "20 sites x 5 individuals"])`
with 20 sites and 5 individuals per population and at least
`r f2(min(res$power_c_design$power.mean[res$power_c_design$design != "20 sites x 5 individuals"]))`
in the other designs, and fell in metacommunities with very low dispersal or with extirpation
when samples were small. The error of $\hat c$ fell mostly with more individuals per
population and more species per site, and the beta diversity of composition did not matter.

Besides sample size, whether $c$ can be identified depends strongly on the width of the
competition kernel relative to the spread of populations in the trait within sites. With a
narrow kernel, few pairs of populations are close enough to push each other, the push hardly
varies among the populations of a species, and $c$ trades off against the kernel width. We
tested this in one cell of the design (dispersal 0.01, patch extirpation 0.01, weak spatial
autocorrelation, $h$ = 0.5) with 20 sites and 5 individuals per population, shrinking the
kernel relative to a fixed spread of 9.8 trait units, the median standard deviation of
population means within sites in one of the metacommunities above (Fig. 2). With a kernel one
fifth of the spread, power for $c$ = 3 was below 0.2 whether the width was estimated or fixed
at its true value. With a kernel half the spread, fixing the width raised power for $c$ = 3
from `r f2(res$narrow$power_free[res$narrow$ratio == 0.5 & res$narrow$c == 3])` to
`r f2(res$narrow$power_fixed[res$narrow$ratio == 0.5 & res$narrow$c == 3])`, and with a kernel
wider than the spread, $c$ = 1 was detected almost always. In the metacommunities above, the
kernel is the niche width, which is wide relative to the spread of optima; this is a choice of
the simulator, not a property of the method. We conjecture that for traits in which
co-occurring species differ far more than any plausible width of a competition kernel, $c$
will not be identifiable with designs of this size, even with the width known.

```{r, fig.cap = "Fig. 2. Power to detect character displacement (c = 1 or 3) as the competition kernel narrows relative to the spread (standard deviation) of population means within sites, with the kernel width estimated or fixed at its true value (20 sites, 5 individuals per population, 60 replicates). Note that fixing the width helps at intermediate widths but not when the kernel is much narrower than the spread."}
n <- res$narrow
n <- rbind(data.frame(n[c("ratio", "c")], width = "estimated", power = n$power_free),
           data.frame(n[c("ratio", "c")], width = "fixed", power = n$power_fixed))
ggplot(n, aes(ratio, power, colour = width, linetype = factor(c))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Kernel width / spread of population means within sites", y = "Power",
       colour = "Kernel width", linetype = "c") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
bt <- res$bootstrap[order(res$bootstrap$c, res$bootstrap$design), ]
small0 <- bt[bt$c == 0 & bt$design == "20 x 5", ]
```

The bootstrap test of `population_shifts()` did not reject too often (Table 3). Without
displacement, it rejected in `r kn(small0$rejection, small0$n)` replicates with the small
design and in none with the large one, so its size was nominal to conservative. With $c$ = 3
it rejected in at least `r round(100 * min(bt$rejection[bt$c == 3]))`% of the replicates, but
its intervals for $c$ covered the true value in fewer than half of them, the corrected
estimate stayed below 3, and the intervals for $h$ covered the true value in only
`r round(100 * min(bt$cover_h))`–`r round(100 * max(bt$cover_h))`% of the replicates. We
therefore read `p_displacement` as the main output and treat the intervals and the corrected
value of $c$ as approximate.

```{r}
knitr::kable(setNames(bt, c("c", "sites x individuals", "replicates", "rejection at 5%",
                            "coverage of c", "coverage of h", "corrected c (median)")),
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("Table 3. Bootstrap test of character displacement in",
                             "population_shifts() (h = 0.5, 99 bootstrap replicates; 95%",
                             "intervals)."))
```

## With full sampling, a PGLS of DR on persistence has no power

Januario et al. (2025) regressed tip speciation rates on metapopulation persistence (logit
equilibrium occupancy, $\varepsilon$, and log turnover, $\tau$) by phylogenetic generalised
least squares (PGLS). We asked whether this kind of regression detects a causal link when one
exists. A latent trait evolved by Brownian motion while lineages speciated at a rate that
increased with it ($\lambda = \lambda_0 e^{bX}$, with $b$ = 0 as the null), until 200 lineages
were alive; the trait set the dispersal of each species in `simulate_metacommunity()`, and
$\varepsilon$ and $\tau$ were estimated from presence over the last 30 steps with a two-state
Markov model. Tip rates were measured with the DR statistic (Jetz et al. 2012) on the
complete tree. Our design differs from theirs, which estimated tip rates on a phylogeny of
thousands of species and then analysed 189 sparsely sampled species, with model selection
among predictors.

Persistence was well estimated ($\tau$ correlated `r f2(min(jd$cor_tau_z))`–`r f2(max(jd$cor_tau_z))`
with the latent trait), and DR was moderately correlated with the true rate (Spearman
correlation `r f2(min(jd$cor_dr_lambda, na.rm = TRUE))`–`r f2(max(jd$cor_dr_lambda, na.rm = TRUE))`).
Nonetheless, the PGLS of log DR on $\varepsilon$ and $\tau$ (a likelihood-ratio test of both)
rejected at about the level of its own slightly inflated size
(`r kn(es_d(0, "pgls_dr"), n_d)` replicates under $b$ = 0), even with $b$ = 1, whereas the
same PGLS on the true rate rejected in almost every replicate with a link (Fig. 3). Our
interpretation, not tested separately, is that DR is the inverse of a weighted sum of branch
lengths along the path to the root, so sister species have the same DR and its signal lies
among clades, while a Brownian PGLS works on contrasts, where DR carries little information.
This mechanism should be weaker when tips are sparsely sampled, as in Januario et al. (2025).

We then applied ES-sim (Harvey & Rabosky 2018) to new replicates of the same design. ES-sim
tests the Pearson correlation between log tip rates and a trait against 999 traits simulated
by Brownian motion on the tree, here two-sided and rejecting at $p \le 0.05$. We report it for $\tau$, the component of
persistence that followed the latent trait, a choice made after seeing the estimates. ES-sim
on $\tau$ detected the link in `r kn(es_d(0.25), n_d)`, `r kn(es_d(0.5), n_d)` and
`r kn(es_d(1), n_d)` replicates for $b$ = 0.25, 0.5 and 1, and rejected in
`r kn(es_d(0), n_d)` without a link, so it was conservative rather than liberal. Testing
$\varepsilon$ and $\tau$ together, with a Bonferroni correction, detected the link in
`r kn(es_d(0.25, "es_any"), n_d)`, `r kn(es_d(0.5, "es_any"), n_d)` and
`r kn(es_d(1, "es_any"), n_d)` replicates. On $\varepsilon$ alone it had no power, because
equilibrium occupancy followed the latent trait poorly (Spearman correlation
`r f2(min(jd$cor_eps_z))`–`r f2(max(jd$cor_eps_z))`). In a negative control, where the trait
set extirpation instead of dispersal and the link to persistence is drowned by demographic
turnover, neither test detected anything. As a result, with a fully sampled clade the absence
of a relationship in a PGLS of DR on persistence is the expected outcome under this model even
with a strong causal link, and a test with a simulation null on the better estimated component
of persistence detects a moderate link. Whether this holds for sparsely sampled tips was not
tested.

```{r, fig.cap = "Fig. 3. Rejection rate at 5% of three tests of the link between persistence and speciation, against the strength of the causal link b (200 replicates per value, window of 30 steps, fully sampled clades). Note that the PGLS on DR stays near its size under b = 0 at every b, while ES-sim on tau approaches the power of the PGLS on the true rate only for b of 0.5 or more."}
e <- es[es$link == "dispersal", ]
e <- rbind(data.frame(b = e$b, test = "PGLS, DR", rejection = e$pgls_dr),
           data.frame(b = e$b, test = "PGLS, true rate", rejection = e$pgls_true),
           data.frame(b = e$b, test = "ES-sim, tau", rejection = e$es_tau))
ggplot(e[!is.na(e$rejection), ], aes(b, rejection, colour = test)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Strength of the link (b)", y = "Rejection rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## What this means

Taken together, the simulations point to one place to look. Branch rates estimated among
species are weakly identified, and an assembly signal planted into them is barely recovered
with trees of 30 species, whereas the same metacommunities leave a clear signal in trait
variation among populations, provided the environment and the local composition enter the
analysis. Moreover, with fully sampled clades, a PGLS of DR on persistence has no power even
under a strong causal link. Our simulations do not test the working hypothesis itself, because
the signal was planted at each scale rather than generated by the dynamics. For empirical
work, the practical consequences are (i) to measure individuals and populations together with
site environment and composition, rather than species means, when the question is about
assembly; (ii) to read the T-statistics only against the species-restricted null and only
together with a model of the environment; (iii) to fix the width of the competition kernel
from independent knowledge when it is of the order of the spread of populations, and to
expect no power for displacement when it is much narrower; and (iv) to test links between tip
rates and species properties with a simulation null rather than a PGLS on DR.

## Limitations

The main limitation is that the signals were planted, not emergent. Local adaptation and
character displacement enter when individuals are sampled and do not evolve during the
dynamics; branch rates come from the turnover of partners through `turnover_rates()`; and the
trait that evolves along the tree is not the trait that is sampled. The experiment therefore
asks how well estimators recover known signals under realistic structures of assembly, not
whether assembly causes the evolution of traits. Answering that needs population traits that
evolve with local selection and gene flow within `simulate_metacommunity()`, and, for the link
studied by Januario et al. (2025), speciation coupled to the metacommunity; both are planned
for a later version of comdynamite. The effect of kernel width was tested in a single cell of
the design and a single sampling design. In the persistence–speciation experiment, the link
from the latent trait to speciation is imposed as a state-dependent process on a continuous
trait, dispersal is the only route from the trait to persistence, detection is perfect, clades
are fully sampled, and tip rates are DR rather than BAMM estimates. ES-sim was implemented here
from its published description, and its size for $\tau$ was
`r kn(es_d(0), n_d)` replicates; we did not check whether a null that also accounts for the
uncertainty in $\tau$ would change this. In the BAMM validation, one of the 20 runs had a low
effective sample size of the log-likelihood (62; 215 or more in the others). Finally, all results come from one simulator, with
niches set by Brownian motion on a single environmental axis.

## Reproducing the results

The simulations are in
[`data-raw/`](https://github.com/diogoprov/comdynamite/tree/main/data-raw):
`validation_rates.R` and `validation_bamm.R` (identifiability), `bridge_experiments.R`,
`bridge_narrow.R` and `bridge_bootstrap.R` (assembly and populations), `januario_power.R` and
`januario_essim.R` (persistence and speciation; the second is a new run with its own seed),
and `vignette_rates_assembly.R`, which builds the summaries shown here. BAMM is a separate GPL
program and was only run, not distributed.
